headline: Business Development & Partnerships at C7
text:
SpaceX now makes up 80% of Saudi Arabia's US stock portfolio
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) has placed a remarkably concentrated bet on Elon Musk's space company. Its latest quarterly 13F filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows that SpaceX now dominates its reported US equity holdings.
The numbers (as of 30 September 2026)
-154.15 million SpaceX shares, worth $23.25 billion
-80.2% of PIF's $28.99 billion in reported US stock holdings
-Nearly five times the value of its next-largest holding, Uber ($4.99 billion)
-Worth more than all its other reported US positions combined

Other holdings
The rest of the portfolio includes Uber, Lucid Group ($721 million) and Claritev (around $27 million). Electronic Arts dropped out after the company was taken private. In the previous quarter, SpaceX made up about 69.5% of the portfolio.

Why it matters
Few sovereign wealth funds put this much of a portfolio into a single company. It shows how strongly PIF believes in SpaceX's long-term value. It's worth keeping in perspective, though: 13F filings cover only reportable US-listed equities, and PIF manages more than $900 billion in total assets.
 
#SpaceX #PIF #SaudiArabia #SovereignWealth #Investing #SEC

text:
The price of industrial power is often the first argument made for a plant in Saudi Arabia. For most manufacturers, it is the smaller lever.

Take a Western European machinery maker. Energy is 0.7 % of its revenue (Eurostat, 2024). In our base case, the lower Saudi tariff adds 0.5 points of profit per EUR 100 of export revenue. Labour adds 9.0.

The labour effect rests on assumptions you set. Our reference labour cost is EUR 9.50 an hour in the Kingdom, against EUR 42.70 in Western European industry (Eurostat, 2025), at 55 % of home productivity. A skilled workforce costs more, and in our conservative case the labour effect is much smaller.

For an Eastern European maker, the labour effect almost disappears: 0.2 points, against 1.4 from energy.

Power becomes a reason of its own in energy-intensive lines. At an energy share of 8 % of revenue, it adds 5.6 points for a Western European plant; at 15 %, it adds 10.5. Saudi Energy's industrial tariff rises from 20 to 23 halalas per kWh on 1 January 2027, which narrows that gain.

What share of your revenue goes on energy?

#SaudiArabia #Manufacturing #Localization

author: Redmond Ramsdale
headline: Head of Middle East Bank Ratings and Islamic Banking at Fitch Ratings
text:
Saudi banking-sector liquidity is expected to remain tight in 2027 as credit demand linked to the country’s economic transformation continues to outpace growth in lower-cost funding sources. Rising reliance on term deposits and wholesale funding is likely to keep funding costs elevated and pressure net financing margins, while prompting banks to become more selective on loan pricing and new lending. Despite tighter liquidity, strong capitalisation and access to domestic and international funding markets should enable banks to continue financing the private sector and Vision 2030 projects, although Fitch Ratings expects credit growth to moderate to 8% in 2027. Banks are also likely to increase their use of bonds, sukuk, certificates of deposit and mortgage securitisations as they diversify funding in Saudi riyals and foreign currencies.

text:
Saudi Arabia’s interest rates are set in Washington.
Right now, Washington is tightening into a Saudi contraction. 📉

Here is the gap in numbers 👇

🏦 The Fed raised rates on 16 September to 3.75–4.00%, its first hike since 2023. Markets now price roughly 96% odds of another 25bp on 9 December.

🇸🇦 SAMA matched it the same day: repo rate 4.50%. The riyal peg leaves little choice.

📊 Meanwhile, GASTAT’s flash estimate shows Saudi real GDP down 3.8% YoY in Q3 2026. Oil activities −20.4%. Non-oil +1.9%.

Two economies. One policy rate.

🔍 What the data says
The US 10-year Treasury yield was 5.12% on 16 November. The 10-year real (inflation-protected) yield: 2.92%.
That real yield is the anchor for every dollar-pegged discount rate in the Gulf.
And it now sits above the real growth rate of Saudi Arabia’s non-oil economy (1.9%).

💰 Why it matters for investors
When the real risk-free rate runs above real growth, valuations do the adjusting, not business plans.

text:
A succession plan can identify who comes next however, does it prepare the business for what comes next?
I’ve been thinking about this since a recent conversation about how family enterprises in the region handle leadership transition. A business can have a plan, a named successor and formal governance, and still not be ready.
The harder questions sit underneath: the knowledge built over decades, the relationships that hold the business together, the judgement behind important decisions, the culture most importantly and who has the authority to act when circumstances change.
I’m in the process of developing a research paper on this, with a focus on GCC family enterprises, and I’d value perspectives from those who have lived through these transitions.

headline: Aspiring CPO | Head of IT Procurement | 28 Yrs Driving $1B+ Tech Spend Across BFSI, Telecom & GCCs | Cloud, SaaS & Managed Services Sourcing
text:
Next time you walk through a tech park in Bengaluru, Hyderabad or Pune, remember this: one in four of the world’s 2,000 biggest companies has a team sitting there.

The Zinnov-Nasscom India GCC Landscape 2026 reports:

▪️ 506 Forbes Global 2000 companies run a Global Capability Centre (GCC) in India

▪️ 2,117 GCCs across 3,728 units

▪️ 2.36 million professionals

▪️ US$98.4 billion in revenue, up 32% since FY21

Most conversations about GCCs focus on talent and cost. As a procurement professional, 
I’d like to point at something else: every one of those centres has to buy things.
Software, cloud, security tools, facilities, telecom links, staffing partners, devices. And a GCC rarely buys the way its parent does.

Here is what makes GCC procurement different, in my view:

Two masters. The parent company sets policy, while the local centre needs speed on the ground.

Fast growth. Headcount can double faster than the supplier base can be organised.

Local rules. Contracts, taxes and data norms in India can differ from the parent’s template.

Maturity varies. The Zinnov data shows only 5% of GCCs have reached the 
“Transformation Hub” stage, while 43% are still “Satellite” centres. Procurement needs differ at each stage.

Having spent 28 years across Banking, Telecom, and Technology, I see GCCs as one of the biggest opportunities for our profession. The centres that get procurement right early save themselves from expensive clean-ups later.

headline: Founder, Krescia & SOREN · Business student at KEDGE · Heading into venture capital in the GCC
text:
I sell to small businesses. So this deal made me smile.

Before Outliers VC invested $300,000 in inve, the fund was inve’s first paying design partner.
Outliers paid for the product first. The cheque came after.

inve is a Saudi event platform. Its founder, Abdulrahman Alabdulkarim, is 23. He built the first version to handle the invitations for his sister’s wedding.
Since then: 250 events, 60+ cities and towns, 35,000+ invitations, an 88% RSVP response rate.

Here is what I think. A fund that pays for the product before it invests tells me more about itself than any thesis on its website.
A pitch deck is a menu. Outliers ate at the restaurant first, and paid the bill.

If you invest at pre-seed in the Gulf: would you pay for the product before you fund it?

text:
🇸🇦 Saudi investors are competing with a US private equity fund to acquire up to an 85% stake in Spanish football club Sevilla, valued at around €500M.

HD Ventures, owned by Saudi brothers Mansour and Haider Sayed, has requested access to Sevilla’s confidential financial information ahead of a potential offer. The brothers previously led an investment group that acquired a 45% stake in English club Crystal Palace in early 2025.

US fund Juggernaut Capital Partners is also considering a bid, with retired Welsh footballer Gareth Bale advising on its sports investments. Goldman Sachs is overseeing the sale process.

Non-binding offers are due by mid-December. A buyer is expected to be selected before the end of 2026, with the ownership transfer targeted for early 2027.

Sevilla is undergoing financial restructuring, with expected losses of €27.4M for the 2025-26 financial year, net debt of around €60M, and a need for at least €80M in new capital.

author: Elie Jahshan
headline: Partnerships @ Jolly | Earn Points at Work
text:
The most important company in gaming doesn’t make a single game.

Silver Lake and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund are in talks to buy Unity.

If you’ve never heard of Unity, you’ve almost definitely played something built on it. 

It's the game building tool behind Pokémon Go and Monopoly Go, and it might sell for $25 billion.

It’s the same group that took EA private for $55 billion just 3 months ago.

Silver Lake isn’t new to Unity either, they already own about 8% of the company. That gave them a front-row seat to Unity’s turnaround.

For years, people said Unity couldn’t make money. Then earlier this month, it posted its first profitable quarter since going public, with $122 million in profit.

So it makes sense that the people closest to the company are the first ones trying to buy it.

I think it’s a smart move. Owning EA gets them the games and Unity gets them the tools thousands of other studios use to build theirs.

So even when someone else makes the hit, Unity’s owners still get paid.

Nothing is signed yet, and the deal could still fall apart.

But if it goes through, the most important company in gaming will belong to the same people who own one of its biggest publishers.

Is gaming turning into a private equity play?

text:
There are 3 ways into the GCC, and each puts a different number on your P&L.
Build (your own subsidiary): you get full control, but you pay for 155 to 405 working days of registration and coverage of about 10,000 Saudi pharmacies before revenue arrives.
Partner (a distributor or licensee): this is the fastest route, but your market position belongs to your partner unless the contract is well governed.
Buy (an acquisition or joint venture): you get instant scale and local manufacturing, but face integration risk in a market where 70% of private-equity deals are now minority stakes.
The right answer depends on 3 numbers:
How much your portfolio could earn in the market at maturity
Your local-manufacturing exposure under Vision 2030
How long you can afford to wait for revenue
Most companies choose a model out of habit. The better ones choose it based on these numbers.
Book a 30-minute GCC Entry Diagnostic. The link is in the comments.

headline: Business Development & Partnerships at C7
text:
SpaceX now makes up 80% of Saudi Arabia's US stock portfolio
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) has placed a remarkably concentrated bet on Elon Musk's space company. Its latest quarterly 13F filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows that SpaceX now dominates its reported US equity holdings.
The numbers (as of 30 September 2026)
-154.15 million SpaceX shares, worth $23.25 billion
-80.2% of PIF's $28.99 billion in reported US stock holdings
-Nearly five times the value of its next-largest holding, Uber ($4.99 billion)
-Worth more than all its other reported US positions combined

Other holdings
The rest of the portfolio includes Uber, Lucid Group ($721 million) and Claritev (around $27 million). Electronic Arts dropped out after the company was taken private. In the previous quarter, SpaceX made up about 69.5% of the portfolio.

Why it matters
Few sovereign wealth funds put this much of a portfolio into a single company. It shows how strongly PIF believes in SpaceX's long-term value. It's worth keeping in perspective, though: 13F filings cover only reportable US-listed equities, and PIF manages more than $900 billion in total assets.
